questions.q: Match each market to its structure.
pairs: Thousands of firms, identical products, free entry
Many firms, slightly different products, easy entry
A few large firms dominate, high barriers
questions.why: Look at the number of firms, how different the product is and how easy entry is.

questions.q: Which set of factors is used to distinguish market structures?
options: Number of firms, product differentiation, ease of entry
questions.why: These three factors separate one structure from another.

questions.q: What is the main effect of successful product differentiation on a firm?
options: Its demand becomes less price elastic
questions.why: Fewer close substitutes means demand is less price elastic, which gives more power over price.

questions.q: Most real-world markets are either perfectly competitive or pure monopolies.
questions.why: These are the two ends of the spectrum. Most real markets sit in between.

questions.q: A town has dozens of hairdressers. Each has its own style, and a new one can open at low cost. Which structure is this closest to?
questions.why: Many firms, differentiated services and low barriers.

questions.q: Explain how the ease of entry into a market affects the profits of firms in that market.

ideas.label: Easy entry attracts new firms when profits are high
This competes profits away, while barriers let firms keep them

questions.model: If entry is easy, high profits attract new firms, which competes the profits away. If there are barriers to entry, firms can keep abnormal profits for longer.
questions.why: Profit is a signal. Barriers decide whether others can answer it.

tests.answer: If entry is easy, new firms join when profits are high and this competes profits away.
New firms will enter the market.
